title: Spring Lecture #30: JPA Relationships
sources: code/jpaRelationshipDemo (model: Student, Department, User, Profile, Student2, Course; repository; service; controller)

questions.question: In the lecture code, `Student` has `@ManyToOne @JoinColumn(name = "dept_id") private Department department;` and `Department` has `@OneToMany(mappedBy = "department") private List<Student> students;`. What does the value `"department"` in `mappedBy` refer to?
options: The foreign-key column `dept_id` in the student table
The name of the department table in the database
The Java field `department` declared in the `Student` entity
The name of a join table that Hibernate creates for the collection
questions.explanation: `mappedBy` names the Java field on the owning entity (`Student.department`) that already maps the relationship. It is not a column name: the column is configured separately via `@JoinColumn(name = "dept_id")`, which is why the two strings differ in the lecture code without any error.

questions.question: Why does a `@ManyToMany` relationship such as Student2 <-> Course need a third table (`student_course`) instead of a single foreign-key column?
options: A single foreign-key column can hold only one referenced id per row, so each (student, course) pair must be stored as its own row with two foreign keys
Hibernate cannot generate foreign keys for entities that use `GenerationType.IDENTITY`
A join table is only needed when the relationship is bidirectional; a unidirectional many-to-many uses a foreign key
Relational databases forbid two tables from referencing each other with foreign keys
questions.explanation: Each row in a table can store only one value in a foreign-key column, but a student has many courses and a course has many students. A join table holds one row per association with `student_id` and `course_id` foreign keys. Direction (uni/bidirectional) only affects Java navigation, not the need for the join table.

questions.question: Student 1 currently has `dept_id = 10`. Department 20 exists. Using the lecture's `Student` mapping (`@ManyToOne @JoinColumn(name = "dept_id")`), what happens when this method runs?
options: Nothing is written, because the student was never passed to `persist()` or a save method after the change
At flush/commit Hibernate issues an UPDATE on the student row setting `dept_id = 20`
Hibernate updates the department row 20 to add the student id to it
Hibernate deletes student 1 and re-inserts it with `dept_id = 20`
questions.explanation: Both entities are managed inside the transaction, so Hibernate's dirty checking compares the student's state at flush time and detects that the owning-side reference changed. It issues an UPDATE of the foreign key `dept_id`; no explicit save is needed for a managed entity. The department table has no column for the relationship, so it is not touched.
questions.source: notes p13 (Update behaviour and dirty checking)

questions.question: The lecture's `Profile` maps `@OneToOne @JoinColumn(name = "user_id") private User user;`. A tester manages to insert two profile rows that both have `user_id = 1`, and the database accepts them. What is the most accurate explanation and fix?
options: `@OneToOne` always creates a unique constraint, so the inserts must have bypassed Hibernate; nothing in the mapping needs changing
The inverse side `User.profile` is missing `cascade = CascadeType.ALL`; adding it blocks the second insert
Because `User` uses `mappedBy`, the `user_id` column is ignored; moving `@JoinColumn` to `User` fixes it
A foreign key alone allows repeated values; one-to-one needs a uniqueness constraint, e.g. `@JoinColumn(name = "user_id", unique = true)`
questions.explanation: In the database, one-to-one is normally 'foreign key + unique constraint'. Without uniqueness the same `user_id` can appear many times, which is effectively one-to-many. Cascade only propagates lifecycle operations and does not add constraints, so it would not prevent duplicate rows.

questions.question: For a mandatory student-department relationship the notes use `@ManyToOne(optional = false)` together with `@JoinColumn(name = "department_id", nullable = false)`. What is the difference between the two settings?
options: `optional = false` says the association is required in the JPA persistence model; `nullable = false` makes the generated FK column NOT NULL in the schema
`optional = false` makes the column NOT NULL; `nullable = false` makes the association load eagerly
They are synonyms; JPA requires both only for backward compatibility
`optional = false` cascades persist to the department; `nullable = false` adds a unique constraint
questions.explanation: The notes describe the two settings as the same rule expressed at different layers: `optional` belongs to the JPA object/persistence model, while `nullable` on `@JoinColumn` affects the generated DDL column. Neither has anything to do with cascading or uniqueness.

questions.question: A teammate replaces `@Getter @Setter @NoArgsConstructor` on the bidirectional `Department` and `Student` entities with `@Data`. Logging a department now crashes with `StackOverflowError`. What is the cause and the safest fix?
options: `@Data` makes all fields final, which breaks Hibernate proxies; add `@NonFinal` to the fields
`@Data` removes the no-args constructor Hibernate needs; add `@NoArgsConstructor` back

The generated `toString()` (and `equals()/hashCode()`) traverse Department -> students -> Student -> department... forever; use explicit `@Getter/@Setter` and exclude relationship fields from those methods
Hibernate cannot load a `List` when Lombok is present; change the collection to a `Set`
questions.explanation: `@Data` generates `toString()`, `equals()` and `hashCode()` over all fields, so a bidirectional pair recurses until the stack overflows (and can also trigger unwanted lazy loads). The notes recommend explicit annotations and excluding relationship fields. `@Data` does not make fields final, and missing constructors would produce an instantiation error, not a stack overflow.

questions.question: Using the lecture's mapping (`Student2.courses` has `@ManyToMany @JoinTable(name = "student_course", ...)`; `Course.students` has `@ManyToMany(mappedBy = "courses")`), student 1 and course 101 already exist. What does this method write to `student_course`?
options: One row (1, 101), because Hibernate detects the change to any managed collection
No row, because only the owning side `Student2.courses` controls the join table and it was not changed
Two rows, one for each side of the bidirectional mapping
It throws an exception because the inverse side collection is read-only
questions.explanation: Hibernate derives join-table rows from the owning side, which is the side with `@JoinTable`. Adding only to the inverse (`mappedBy`) collection changes the in-memory graph but not the database, and it does not throw either. The fix is a helper such as `addCourse()` that updates `courses` and `course.getStudents()` together.

questions.question: The goal is a shared-primary-key one-to-one: `profiles.id` must equal the owning user's `id` and also act as the foreign key to `users.id`. Which change makes this mapping express that intent correctly?
options: Replace `@MapsId` with `mappedBy = "profile"` so the user's id is copied into the profile
Add `unique = true` to `@JoinColumn`, since `@MapsId` alone cannot guarantee one profile per user
Change `@OneToOne` to `@ManyToOne`, because `@MapsId` only works on many-to-one
Remove `@GeneratedValue`: with `@MapsId` the profile's id is taken from the associated user, not generated
questions.explanation: With `@MapsId` the child's identifier is derived from the associated parent, so it must be a plain `@Id` without a generator, exactly as in the notes. `unique = true` is redundant because the shared column is already the primary key, and `mappedBy` would turn this side into the inverse side, which cannot supply the id.

questions.question: The lecture code maps `Student2.courses` as a `List<Course>` with `@JoinTable(name = "student_course", joinColumns = ..., inverseJoinColumns = ...)`. A double-clicked 'Enroll' button calls `student.getCourses().add(java)` twice, and two identical (1, 101) rows appear. Which change best follows the notes to prevent this?
options: Add `cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST` so Hibernate checks for existing rows before inserting
Swap `joinColumns` and `inverseJoinColumns` so the course becomes the owning side
Use a `Set<Course>` and add `uniqueConstraints = @UniqueConstraint(columnNames = {"student_id", "course_id"})` to `@JoinTable`
Mark the `Course.students` side with `mappedBy` so only one row can be written
questions.explanation: Each join-table row is one enrollment, so the (student_id, course_id) pair should be unique at the database level, and a `Set` avoids duplicate elements in memory. Cascade only propagates lifecycle operations to the Course entity; it does not de-duplicate association rows. `Course.students` already uses `mappedBy`, so that changes nothing.

questions.question: A teammate says: "`Department` is the parent, so if I put `cascade = CascadeType.ALL` on `@OneToMany(mappedBy = "department")`, Department becomes the owning side and `department.getStudents().add(s)` alone will set `dept_id`." What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Cascading only propagates lifecycle operations (persist, remove, ...); ownership is decided by `mappedBy`/`@JoinColumn`, so `Student.department` still controls `dept_id`
Nothing is wrong; cascade on the parent makes it the owning side as long as `mappedBy` is present
Cascade makes Department the owning side, but only for inserts, not for updates
`CascadeType.ALL` is not allowed on a `mappedBy` collection, so the code will not start
questions.explanation: The notes stress that owning side does not mean parent, and that cascading controls lifecycle propagation, not ownership. The `mappedBy` side is always the inverse side, so with cascade the new student may be persisted but its `dept_id` stays NULL unless `student.setDepartment(...)` is also called. Cascade on a `mappedBy` collection is perfectly legal.
questions.source: notes p8 (Owning side), p27 (Core principles 5 and 10)
